> ### ⚠️ SUPERSEDED IN PART — read [the correction](https://github.com/HiQS-Labs/Needle-fork/issues/12#issuecomment-5596333076) first
>
> Three claims in the Evidence and "What this invalidates" sections below are **withdrawn**:
> the MLX-vs-engine comparison is **unpaired** (disjoint row sets, zero overlap); "100% well-formed"
> is really a **name-extraction rate**; and "PTQ was never the cause" **overcorrected** (D7's
> MLX-side PTQ degeneracy is still unexplained). The tool-declaration probe's 37.5% row also
> carries a **position confound** — gold was always listed first.
>
> The root-cause conclusion stands, but on **different evidence** than the argument below produced:
> a direct KV-accounting sweep showing the engine's prefix collapses to 0 at ≥6 declared tools with
> turn length saturating (6 and 10 tools → identical 352 tokens). See the correction comment.
>
> Numbers below are retained unedited for audit. A re-run on a frozen shared manifest is pending.

> **This issue body was rewritten on 2026-09-08 before any advisor read it.** The original
> framing ("QAT failed to close a native-engine quantisation gap") rested on two measurement
> defects and was wrong. Nothing below is inherited from it. The original text is preserved in
> the edit history. Recording the supersession rather than silently swapping it, per SOP §5.7.

## Summary

The Oracle's deployed numbers were never measuring the model. Two independent defects, both in
the measurement/serving path, not in training or quantisation:

1. **The engine serves only 5 of the 44 declared tools.** It runs a tool-retrieval step; above
   five declared tools only the five highest-scoring enter context, and the vendor README states
   plainly that *"an unselected tool is unreachable."* The Oracle declares 44 and was **trained**
   with all 44 schemas in the prompt (1,383 tokens of schemas; the engine's cached prefix is
   **234 tokens**). The retrieval head is the base checkpoint's — LoRA never touched it.
2. **The eval harness reused one engine across rows.** The engine is conversational: each
   `complete()` continues the prior turn, so after the assistant emits a tool call the next call
   replies instead of calling. Perfect `Y n Y n` alternation, discarding every second prediction.
   `needle_reset()` exists and `complete()` never calls it.

Together these account for most of the "deployed collapse" that #5's D7 → D8 → D9 chain was built
to explain. The model and the LoRA fine-tune are demonstrably fine (21.67% generating on MLX).
**One residual is not yet explained — see "Open question" below.**

## Evidence

Same 200 seed-0 holdout rows; native-engine rows use a fresh engine per row (defect 2 removed).

| path | top-1 | note |
|---|---|---|
| static majority baseline | 12.50% | 16.30% at n=1000 |
| QAT adapter — **MLX generation** (the engine's exact task, same weights, same QAT numerics) | **21.67%** | n=60, 100% parse, 100% well-formed |
| QAT adapter — MLX ranking (P(label\|prompt), 44 candidates) | 19.00% | |
| base — MLX generation | 10.00% | n=60, 43% parse |
| base — native engine | 7.00% | 79% answered |
| **2k adapter (D7's artifact), PTQ — native engine** | **12.00%** | 100% answered |
| QAT adapter — **native engine** | **3.00%** | 100% answered |

Same weights, same numerics, same task: **21.67% on MLX vs 3.00% through the engine.**

Tool-declaration probe (QAT `.cact`, 40 rows, fresh engine per row):

| declared | answered | top-1 |
|---|---|---|
| all 44 (as trained) | 100% | 5.0% |
| 5, gold **included** | 100% | **37.5%** |
| 5, gold **excluded** | 100% | **0.0%** |

The 0.0% is the mechanism: an undeclared label cannot be emitted. The 37.5% is oracle-assisted
(gold is guaranteed present) so it is an upper bound, not a shippable number — but it establishes
that reachability, not model quality, is the binding constraint.

Alternation (defect 2), 24 rows: reused engine `Y n Y n ...` → 12/24 answered; `reset()` between
rows → 24/24; fresh engine per row → 24/24, identical predictions.

## What this invalidates

- **D7 ("PTQ destroys the fine-tune")** — unsound. Its headline number came from the broken
  harness, and its causal claim is contradicted by the base control: the *untuned* base scores
  **higher** through the engine (7.0%) than the tuned artifact (3.0%). PTQ was never the cause.
- **D9 ("QAT does not close the deployment gap")** — the specific comparison it drew was a
  metric-mixing error on my part (QAT's top-1-overall against PTQ's precision-when-answering).
  On a clean harness the honest comparison is **PTQ 12.0% vs QAT 3.0%** — so QAT did not merely
  fail to help, the QAT artifact is materially *worse* through the engine, which D9 asserted for
  the wrong reason and with the wrong numbers.
- **D8's parity gate** — verified MLX against JAX; neither was ever verified against the native
  engine, which is where the gap lives. The QAT port is numerically correct by that gate and
  generates well on MLX (21.67%), yet its exported artifact is the worst performer through the
  engine. Correct work, but it did not address the actual defect.
- **`eval_cact.py`'s "precision when answering"** — the sample contains zero abstention rows, so
  that metric conditioned away half the failures and should not have been offered as a bar.

## Open question (new, unexplained)

On a clean harness the three artifacts rank: **2k PTQ 12.0% > base 7.0% > 10k QAT 3.0%** — while
on MLX the QAT adapter generates at 21.67%. Retrieval alone does not explain this: all three
declare the same 44 tools and should be equally throttled. Something about the QAT artifact
specifically degrades through the engine while being fine in MLX. Candidates, none tested:
tool retrieval scores tools using the model's own representations (which LoRA *does* alter, and
10k QAT alters more than 2k fp32); or the QAT export interacts with the engine's decode
differently. **This is the sharpest open thread and probably the next experiment.**

Note this also means D7's artifact, measured properly, sits **at** the 12.5% static baseline
rather than far below it — so "PTQ destroys the fine-tune" was an artifact of the broken harness
in both its number and its conclusion.

## The actual fork

The Oracle's contract (44 mutually-exclusive labels, pick one) is not what this engine serves
(retrieve ≤5 tools, then call one). Candidate directions:

1. **Fit the contract: ≤5 declared tools.** Score the existing artifact with a fixed top-5 label
   set (covers ~62% of rows), no retrieval involved. Cheap, and directly measurable now.
2. **One tool, label as an enum argument.** Collapses 44 tools to a single declared tool whose
   argument is the label — sidesteps retrieval entirely. Needs a corpus re-render and a retrain.
3. **Fix retrieval's blindness.** The retrieval head is untuned base; LoRA never touched it.
   Unclear if it is trainable through the available surface.
4. **Serve without this engine.** MLX in-process already delivers 21.67%. Crosses the documented
   "MLX is never a dependency of `main`" boundary (GH-5 Bounds, `ROADMAP.md:23`,
   `spike/mlx/README.md`), and costs ~550 MB of deps vs 28 MB, 14.8 s/row.
5. **Descope to base through the engine** — measured at 7.0%, *below* the 12.5% static baseline.
   Ships a regression; listed only to be ruled out.

## Ask

Which fork, and why. Note that (1) is measurable today against work already on disk, and that
(2) is the only option that makes the task and the engine agree by construction.

Two independent investigations (this session, and a separately-prompted Fable agent working the
same problem) converged on the retrieval finding from different evidence — engine probes and
`strings` on the closed dylib on one side, controlled tool-declaration experiments on the other.
The alternation defect was found on only one side, and Fable's grammar-related `[]` numbers are
likely contaminated by it.

Receipts: `data/spike-mlx/logs/eval-cact-{10k-qat,base,2k}-FRESH.json`,
`gen-probe-{10k-qat,base}.json`, `eval-oracle-10k-qat-mlx.json`. Full history: #5.
Detailed options writeup: `PROJECT/1-INBOX/GH-5-NEXT-STEPS-D9.md`.

title: Root cause: the engine serves only 5 of 44 declared tools — the Oracle's contract is unservable as built
